explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on “marker” tokens—those compact, low‐frequency symbols or strings that often serve structural or emphasis roles across languages.  Examples include uppercase or abbreviated English segments (ESS, Feb), enumeration dots and hyphens (・, in-between parts of hyphenated words), single‐character script tokens (Katakana ン, Chinese 号, Tamil letters, Hangul fragments), and similar one‐ or two‐character markers that punctuate text, list items, dates or code.

This feature fires on the final token of headings, titles or labeled sections (e.g. headlines, subheads, menu links) in news-style or web-article text—essentially marking the boundary where a prominent title or label ends and the body copy begins.

This feature fires on the punctuation that terminates standalone header-style lines—titles, disclaimers, calls-to-action or metadata entries—marking the end of a block or section across UI messages, legal citations, code/license headers, etc.

This neuron lights up on the “head” sub‐token of multi‐part technical terms across whatever domain it’s reading—i.e. the very first piece of a compound identifier or keyword (CSS property names like “color,” CMake variables like “LIST,” Java getters like “get…,” chemical substituent markers like position numbers “4,” “6,” suffixes like “yl,” or domain labels like “St” in Stakes/Stocks, etc.). In short, it flags the opening subword of domain‐specific compound tokens.
This feature detects the use of “2” as an ordinal or list‐item marker (e.g. “2)”, “2.”, “2/5”)—i.e. the label for the second element in numbered sections or lists.

This feature consistently lights up on section‐level headers or titles across domains — e.g. block-comment file headers (/* … */), copyright banners, court-docket headings (“No. …”, “Accepted”), application or news article titles, blog post headlines, etc. It’s a general “section title/header” detector.

This feature lights up on those tiny subwords or single-token “qualifiers” that carry semantic force at the ends (or on their own) of identifiers and literals—things like unit or dimension suffixes (m in p.m., d in bg3d), numeric indices or version tags (40, 17, e11), boolean flags (false), axis labels (y), annotation keywords (pragma), etc. It’s essentially a detector for the short, often one- or two-subword pieces that act as semantic modifiers or flags in code and technical writing.
This feature detects the comment‐block delimiters and boilerplate that mark a file’s license/header section (e.g. /**, //, **/, copyright lines, license names and separators).

This neuron fires on “structural” tokens in code/markup—things like file‐extension strings (jpg, hpp), URL schemes (http), XML/HTML tag delimiters (>), sequences of semicolons, and standalone numeric identifiers—i.e. metadata or syntax markers rather than natural-language words.

This neuron fires on the first substantive token of a formal section or document heading—e.g. the opening word of a legal‐case caption (“IN THE UNITED STATES COURT …,” docket numbers like “426”), the leading term of a paper title (“Variations,” “Survival,” “Differential …,” “Different …”), publication status headers (“UNPUBLISHED”), location qualifiers (“D.C.”), news headlines (“Don’t undermine …”), the name in a mythological title (“Anna Perenna”), or the opening article word in German news (“Der 1. FC Köln …”). In short, it detects the token that begins a new top‐level heading or title block across varied text genres.

This feature fires on tokens that begin new structural blocks—section titles or headings and their metadata (e.g. names, dates, archive labels, code-import lines). In other words, it detects the start-of-heading/section markers in text.

This feature is a non-finite-verb marker detector in formal/technical prose: it lights up on the infinitive “to” and the auxiliary “be” (often with modals like can/will) that introduce purpose or passive clauses (e.g. “to make,” “can be changed,” “will be held”).

explanations.explanation: This neuron picks out the small “linking” words—mostly prepositions (of, over, with, by, on, in) plus the occasional that/method—used in technical Q&A to signal comparisons, sources or provenance, instruments, locations, and other logical or causal relationships.

This neuron seems to fire on structural‐metadata markers – the little tokens that introduce or delimit sections or notes.  In Japanese news copy it lights up on the first character of header labels like 更新 (“update”) or 特記 (“special note”), in code comments on the /**…*/ delimiters or the final period after “Authors.” in license blocks, and even on emphasis markers in markdown.  In short, it’s looking for section-heading or metadata-boundary tokens.

This neuron appears to be signaling the end-of-line boundary of standalone banner/headline/disclaimer snippets—short, self-contained UI or editorial lines (e.g. “Register Now,” cookie-consent notices, newsletter opt-in blurbs, section titles, news headlines, license comment headers) that terminate with distinctive punctuation or formatting before the main body.
This neuron fires on tokens that are pure digit‐sequences or primarily numeric (dates, measurements, CSS/HTML sizes, stats, IDs, etc.), i.e. it flags number tokens across contexts.

The feature fires whenever the model sees the very first sub‐token of a “salient” or specialized term—whether that’s a CamelCase identifier (Squiz, Splines, Nightscout), an acronym (DME, GPT, D7), a proper name (Hopsin, BERNER) or other technical/jargon word. In effect it flags the onset of code names, acronyms and domain‐specific vocabulary.

This feature is essentially a “start‐of‐segment” detector – it lights up on the pair of special/newline tokens that kick off every new paragraph, heading or document chunk (i.e. the two tokens just before the first real word of a section).

This neuron fires on tokens that mark the start of a new structural unit—whether a sentence or clause boundary (“.”, “,”, “but”, “and”, “to”, “hence”, “soon”, “seems”), the head of a list or numeric index (“18:4”, “599,”, “11|…”), or the key‐name in code blocks/JSON/CSS (“alias”, “border”, “line”). In other words, it detects tokens that introduce a fresh segment—be it a new clause, list item, or code/property declaration.

This neuron acts as a detector for the terminal “.” – the full-stop punctuation that closes out sentences, headings, file names/extensions, section numbers or other structural units in technical or formal writing.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is basically a prefix detector: it lights up on the first one to three letters at the start of content words (URLs, technical terms, proper names, medical jargon, etc.), regardless of their meaning, signaling “here comes a new token.”

This neuron flags the front‐matter or header of a document—that is, the opening title/metadata lines (court captions, “UNPUBLISHED” notices, copyright lines, article or news headlines, transcript disclaimers, etc.). It marks the start of a new section or document.
This neuron lights up on the first, capitalized word of a news‐style headline or section title—i.e. the lead token that kicks off an article or subheading.

This feature fires on hyphen‐bound morphemes in technical/academic compounds—i.e. the hyphens (and attached ordinal or edition suffixes) that link numeric, dimensional or “non-” prefixes to nouns/adjectives (15-year, 3-dimensional, non-culturable, 2nd Edition, etc.).

This feature fires on the little “definition‐or‐naming” markers in formal/technical prose—words and punctuation like “called,” “termed,” “originally,” “as,” “to,” or a colon when you introduce or define a concept or list. It flags the moment you’re naming or defining something.

This feature fires on the kind of fixed‐form “legal/metadata” headers you see at the top of source files or court opinions—e.g. comment delimiters plus copyright/license blocks (GNU/Apache, “DO NOT EDIT,” “Licensed under…,” etc.) or official case headings (“IN THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS,” “Opinions of the United States…”).

This neuron fires on “specification language” in technical or scientific prose—i.e. the qualifiers and units that precisely constrain or qualify something (adjectives like appropriate, suitable, desired, narrow; locative descriptors like intracellular; measurement terms/units and their markers such as of, cm, bp, micron, ounce; even adjectival suffixes like –iant or –ucent).

explanations.explanation:
Here’s a concise concept for each highlighted feature:

• **eno** (in “Ken Cedeno/UPI | License Photo”): marks UPI‐style photo byline credits in news text (the photographer’s surname fragment).  
• **2** (in `#include <opencv2/...>`): signals version‐numbered C/C++ header paths (e.g. OpenCV “2”).  
• **pointer** (in a `typedef … pointer;` inside lycon headers): picks out C++ type‐alias definitions using the word “pointer.”  
• **US** (in AWS Markdown links like “en-US/User Guide”): identifies locale or country codes (“US”) in documentation URLs.  
• **ier** (in “Multiplier” and similar): detects the common “-ier” suffix in code identifiers.  
• **/F** (in expressions like “V/F” or “D/F”): flags slash‐followed‐by–variable notation (per‐unit ratios) in analytics formulas.  
• **code** (in PHP test arrays like `['code' => 200]`): spots the HTTP-status‐code key in mock response fixtures.  
• **al** (in “et al.”): recognizes the “et al.” citation pattern in scientific writing.  
• **)** (in list markers like “2)”): fires on closing‐parenthesis list delimiters in Markdown or plain-text outlines.  
• **0** (in PowerShell version strings like “MajorVersion = $(version.Major).0”): picks up zero as a minor‐version component in build scripts.  
• **s** (in units like “erg s⁻¹” or “erg/s”): detects “per-second” unit notation in scientific formulas.  
• **2** (in “mg/m²” dosage): marks the superscript-2 (squared) unit notation in medical and scientific text.  
• **\/** (in code like `add_filter('pre_http_request', …)` or regexes): recognizes an escaped forward slash sequence (“\/”).  
• **ke** (in include paths like `"drake/common/…"`): flags the “ke” fragment from the Drake library path in C++ imports.  
• **f** (in cluster logs at “ocf::heartbeat”): spotlights the “f” in the “ocf::” prefix of Pacemaker resource-agent names.

This feature marks the very first character of a structural token—e.g. the “<” that opens an HTML/XML tag, or the initial letter/digit of an identifier, namespace segment, component name or acronym right after a separator.

This neuron is a structural marker for blog‐ or news‐style entries: it spikes on the headline (titles, dates, names, list‐item headings) and again on the very first token of the paragraph that follows.

This feature detects formal metadata boilerplate—tokens you find in license and copyright headers, corporate registration notices or academic funding acknowledgments. It lights up on organization names, license/version numbers, registration numbers and grant‐funding language.
This feature fires on the very first word of a title or section heading—across patents, papers, news, fiction or tweets—essentially marking the start‐of‐heading token.

This feature picks out small, frequently occurring subword chunks—both affix‐like letter sequences (e.g. pro-, ­ing, ­ous, ­arm, ­ung, ­ird) and function connectors (and, ’s, the digit “1”) as well as punctuation delimiters (. , – / \\)—that serve as structural or morphological boundaries in code, file paths, URLs and technical English terms.

This feature appears to detect syntactic‐discourse boundary markers—i.e. tokens that signal transitions between segments—such as introductory prepositions (“for,” “of”), delimiting punctuation (commas, apostrophes), and uppercase initials that begin names or titles.

explanations.explanation: This neuron isn’t about any particular topic but rather about the little “glue” of language and code—prepositions (“to”), sequence markers (“next,” “first,” “default”), and the fragments and punctuation of English contractions (the “don-,” “‘t,” “does-,” “‘m,” etc.) or code delimiters like “(”.  In other words, it fires on high-frequency functional tokens and punctuation that stitch sentences or statements together rather than on substantive content words.

This feature detects front-matter section headers or metadata markers—e.g. docket numbers and underscored separators in legal opinions, “UNPUBLISHED” or “NOT RECOMMENDED” labels, news datelines (MANILA, Oct. 16, 2017), bylines or photo credits (Reuters), entry titles (People v Shimburski; Henri Valois), book or article headings (“THE FOURTH WATCH,” “Stay in the loop,” “Archive for 2013”), and similar uppercase/title tokens that signal the start of a structured document section.

This neuron fires on the little “non-ordinary” bits that structure technical notation across domains—things like command-line flags (-r), braces or underscores in code/markup, hyphens in identifiers, and specialized affixes or prefixes/suffixes in chemistry or biology (dimethyl-, amino-, ‑ense in missense, etc.). It marks the punctuation and morphemes that frame domain-specific syntax rather than ordinary prose.

This feature fires on tokens that mark the start of a new section or title—e.g. document headings, paper section titles, email headers, legal‐docket headings or news datelines—i.e. structural “heading” cues.
